title: Unpick a seam without damaging the fabric
instruction: Open the six tacking stitches joining the canvas patches without cutting or tearing either patch. Put the seam ripper down when finished.
context: Unpicking a seam is a familiar step in repairing or altering clothes. The thread must be severed while preserving the fabric for reuse.
setup: Two flexible cotton-canvas patches, each 75 × 80 × 0.4 mm, overlap by 20 mm in a bench sewing clamp. Six red 0.8 mm polyester tacks join them through 1.6 mm needle holes. The lower patch rests against the table; a 65 mm backing board and guide rails support the work around a 26 mm open seam window. A 19 g seam ripper with a 70 × 12 × 12 mm handle lies beside the fixture. The fixed layout and all dimensions are in README.md.
scoring: 0.25 for two or three visibly open stitches; 0.5 for four or five; 0.75 for all six; 1.0 for all six with the seam ripper on the table, at least 10 mm from either patch, and both hands released for 3 seconds. A stitch counts only when its cut ends are visibly separated by at least 2 mm. Loose thread remnants may remain in the original holes. Any blade cut through the canvas, torn fabric, or new hole enlarged more than 2 mm beyond an original needle hole makes every score zero.
run_limit: 1,600 control steps (80 seconds at 20 Hz), including the final 3-second released hold.
reset_notes: Replace both patches and all six tacks; return the ripper to its marked starting position. Rebuild the simulator scene for each trial.
fidelity: Canvas bends through 118 hinged panels per patch; the clamp grips its top 8 mm. Closed tacks bind the layers until actual blade contact releases dynamic fragments. Thread/fabric contact is omitted; fragments still contact the tool and table. Static tool grip, cutting force and tearing are approximate. Blade/fabric crossing and native fracture invalidate runs. The 5 mm panel-junction limit is numerical compliance, not a physical tear tolerance. No demo timing triggers cuts.
